stances.claim: Trump's four criminal indictments are historic (the first US president, incumbent or past, to be charged criminally, and the only one arrested at the instance of a grand jury and given an inmate number) but will only 'interfere, for better or for worse' with his 2024 campaign -- they will not settle the question.

'Far more crucial' than the four criminal indictments is Trump's potential disqualification under the 14th Amendment Section 3 -- the constitutional question of whether someone who 'engaged in insurrection or rebellion against the [US]' may hold any public office.
stances.rhetorical_move: redirection-of-attention (the bigger question is constitutional, not criminal)

stances.claim: A verba legis reading of Section 3 would disqualify Trump for his alleged Jan. 6 participation in the 'rebellious' conspiracy to prevent the Biden proclamation.

A ratio legis reading may save Trump because the Amendment's intent was specifically to bar defeated Confederate officers post-Civil War; that purpose has long been accomplished (functus officio), and applying the provision today extends it beyond its historical purpose.
stances.rhetorical_move: intent-and-purpose framing (introducing functus officio doctrine into US constitutional reading)
stances.confidence: presented as a competing valid reading

stances.claim: The disqualification will become ripe only when Trump is nominated and state electoral officials refuse to include his electors on the ballot -- the procedural pathway through which the question reaches Scotus.
stances.rhetorical_move: procedural-ripeness framing (explaining when the legal question becomes live)

stances.claim: The case will 'test the philosophical leanings' of the nine Scotus justices -- six Republican-appointed verba legis adherents vs three Democratic-appointed ratio legis adherents -- making this a doctrinal test as much as a political one.
The world is watching whether the US 'will uphold the rule of law or succumb to the rule of the mob' -- locating the Trump cases in the global rule-of-law conversation, not just US domestic politics.

notable_anecdotes: Trump's Fulton County jail booking: detained at 'the notoriously dingy Fulton County Jail in Atlanta, Georgia,' given inmate number P01135809, released 30 minutes later on $200,000 bail bond -- his 'historic scowling mug shot' taken 'like any other defendant.'
Post-release Trump quote: 'What has taken place here is a travesty of justice. I did nothing wrong' -- 'bowled unbowed.'

Co-accused roster includes Mark Meadows ('equivalent to our executive secretary') and Rudy Giuliani -- CJ uses parallel translations to make US offices intelligible to Filipino readers (Giuliani 'as former mayor of New York City, became an international sensation for ridding the city that never sleeps of criminality and vandalism').
Al Capone reference for context on RICO: Georgia's RICO Act 'is similar to a federal law to fight organized crime groups (like that of the infamous Al Capone in the late 1920s and early 1930s).'

Three other cases catalogued: NY hush-money for an 'alleged porn star,' FL mishandling of top-secret state documents, DC Jan. 6 Capitol 'rebellious' undertaking -- CJ uses the same 'rebellious' descriptor that 14th Amendment Section 3 echoes.

Aug. 31, 2023: Trump pleaded not guilty 'in writing and in absentia' to avoid media cameras and asked for trial postponement until after the November 2024 elections -- CJ reads this as fear of being exposed 'as a felon to his avowed critics' though he 'may remain a hero to his diehard supporters.'

Procedural-pathway projection: 'should he be nominated -- any of the electoral officials of the 50 US states may refuse to include him (or more precisely, his electors) from the ballot' -- CJ correctly anticipates the Trump v. Anderson pathway that would reach Scotus in early 2024.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban catalogues Donald Trump's historic status as the first and only American president -- incumbent or past -- to be criminally indicted, not once but four times: the Fulton County RICO case under DA Fani T. Willis (a 97-page indictment alleging criminal conspiracy to overturn Georgia's 2020 results, with 18 co-accused including chief of staff Mark Meadows and lawyer Rudy Giuliani, and explicitly likened to the federal RICO statute used against Al Capone), the New York hush-money case for an alleged porn star, the Florida case for mishandling top-secret state documents, and the Washington DC conspiracy in the Jan. 6, 2021 'rebellious' undertaking to prevent the proclamation of Biden. CJ notes that Trump alone was arrested at a grand jury's instance and detained at 'the notoriously dingy Fulton County Jail' with inmate number P01135809 before $200,000 bail and his 'historic scowling mug shot,' then 'bowled unbowed': 'What has taken place here is a travesty of justice. I did nothing wrong.' But CJ argues that 'far more crucial' than the four criminal cases is Trump's possible disqualification under the 14th Amendment Section 3 -- and presents the verba legis reading (his alleged Jan. 6 participation suffices) against the ratio legis reading (the Amendment targeted post-Civil War Confederate officers and may be functus officio). The question is not yet ripe because Trump is only seeking the Republican nomination; but should he be nominated, state electoral officials may refuse to include his electors on the ballot, sending the case to a Scotus where the six Republican-appointed (verba legis) justices and the three Democratic-appointed (ratio legis) justices will face a doctrinal test as much as a political one. CJ closes with the global stakes: 'Will the US uphold the rule of law or succumb to the rule of the mob? The world is keenly watching!'
